section_summary: This section follows American, British, and Dutch efforts to respond to Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, especially its six-month oil stock requirement and its effects on foreign companies. Embassy reports, company correspondence, and State Department conversation records discuss possible joint diplomatic action, company negotiations, and a proposed oil monopoly in Manchuria. Several telegrams and Mukden despatches appear in duplicate.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle on Japanese petroleum policy, concluding pages
subfiles.about: Hornbeck urges oil companies to decide how they will respond to Japan’s petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Teagle awaits a London conference with Deterding before choosing a course. Hornbeck discusses refusal to comply, possible Japanese reactions, and the difficulty of coordinating independent oil producers.

subfiles.title: Analysis of Tokyo telegram No. 241
subfiles.about: The division assesses Japan’s reply to foreign representations on the petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Japan offers assurances about existing quotas and market-price purchases but leaves the crucial storage requirement unaddressed. The memorandum recommends awaiting the oil companies’ responses.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 241, first copy
subfiles.about: Grew summarizes Japan’s informal reply to American petroleum-law representations.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains annual licensing, quota allocation, refining permits, and pricing. It says nothing about the six-month stock requirement.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 241, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy repeats Grew’s summary of Japan’s reply.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the licensing, quota, refining, and pricing points, with no answer on six-month oil stocks.

subfiles.title: Parker letter quoting Goold’s November 2 cable
subfiles.about: Parker reports Goold’s view that Japan’s reply is unsatisfactory.
subfiles.summary: Parker quotes Goold’s cable and asks about a State Department telegram to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply to Parker
subfiles.about: Hornbeck explains that Washington awaits a company plan and British initiative.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges Parker’s letter and clarifies the Department’s November 1 message to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Far Eastern Affairs note
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten note refers to a conversation.
subfiles.summary: The substantive text cannot be reliably recovered from the OCR.

subfiles.title: Routing comment on Tokyo despatch No. 1017
subfiles.about: A reader recommends despatch No. 1017 for background on Japan’s official oil position.
subfiles.summary: Notes that the despatch contains little new information but useful background.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1017: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Grew reports foreign representations and the oil companies’ refusal to file complete storage plans.
subfiles.summary: British representatives renewed their appeal to Japan. Standard-Vacuum and Rising Sun filed sales plans but withheld import and storage plans; Japanese officials demanded completion, exposing Standard-Vacuum to possible license cancellation and a fine. Grew encloses the British aide-memoire, Japan’s demand letter, and Dickover’s conversation with Kurusu.

subfiles.title: British Embassy aide-memoire
subfiles.about: Britain asks Japan to relieve petroleum companies of hardships under the new law.
subfiles.summary: Requests clarification or modification so British firms can decide their business policy and meet filing requirements.

subfiles.title: Mining Bureau demand for a supplementary business-plan report
subfiles.about: The Mining Bureau asks Standard-Vacuum to complete its 1935 business-plan application.
subfiles.summary: Calls the September 28 application incomplete and requests an urgent supplement.

subfiles.title: Dickover–Kurusu conversation
subfiles.about: Dickover asks Kurusu what will happen if foreign oil companies reject Japan’s stock requirement.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu considers reduced quotas, amendment of the law, or company withdrawal, but sees serious practical problems with each. He agrees that six months of additional reserves would be costly and describes the law as unworkable. The two also discuss employment, existing investment, and who should finance national oil reserves.

subfiles.title: Teagle letter on proposed joint representations
subfiles.about: Teagle relays a London proposal for three governments to approach Japan jointly.
subfiles.summary: The proposed approach seeks a clear Japanese statement and talks with foreign oil companies.

subfiles.title: Walden cable on proposed Manchurian oil monopoly
subfiles.to: G. S. Walden, New York; P. W. Parker
subfiles.about: The cable relays a Mukden account of a proposed Manchukuo petroleum monopoly.
subfiles.summary: The reported scheme would combine Fushun and Dairen output with quota purchases from importers and replace existing brands. Companies are asked for sales and equipment information by November 15; the cable urges prompt opposition.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck–Teagle telephone conversation
subfiles.about: Hornbeck discusses possible coordinated diplomatic action with Teagle.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says Washington would consider British or Dutch suggestions sympathetically, while timing and company plans require thought. Teagle agrees to convey that position to his London associates.

subfiles.title: Teagle letter on withdrawal and negotiations
subfiles.about: Teagle shares company cables debating withdrawal from Japan and talks with Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: One cable suggests coordinated refusal to comply might produce a settlement. London associates consider withdrawal premature and prefer joint governmental representations followed by negotiations with the two principal foreign companies.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck–Teagle conversation on company plans
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks what the oil companies would ultimately do if negotiations fail.
subfiles.summary: He says Washington could likely join a request for company talks with Japan, but expects the British side to initiate any joint governmental proposal. Teagle agrees to repeat this in London.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck conversations with Teagle, Parker, and Coe
subfiles.about: Hornbeck records company planning and exchanges with three Standard-Vacuum representatives.
subfiles.summary: Teagle seeks a common company program and waits for London’s response. Parker may travel to Tokyo, while Coe supplies a cable describing planned company representatives. Hornbeck repeats that Washington awaits both a clear company position and British governmental initiative.

subfiles.title: Harden cable quoted in company memorandum
subfiles.from: P. W. Parker, quoting O. C. Harden
subfiles.about: The cable proposes diplomatic representations before oil-company negotiations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: It reports plans for Walden, Godber, and Parker to reach Japan in December.

subfiles.title: Coe letter explaining Standard-Vacuum’s position
subfiles.about: Coe explains the company’s opposition to financing Japan’s required oil reserves.
subfiles.summary: Clarifies its August representations, incomplete 1935 form, and the roles of Shell and Standard-Vacuum directors.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable of November 2
subfiles.about: The company reports Japan’s unsatisfactory reply and contrasts foreign firms’ positions on stock compliance.
subfiles.summary: It says Standard-Vacuum has explicitly opposed the stock requirement, while its counterpart has sought more time to complete its form.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgement to Coe
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Coe’s letter and Yokohama cable.
subfiles.summary: Says the Department is considering the company’s August 31 representations.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Baltimore Sun article
subfiles.about: A newspaper article on Japanese oil policy is sent to Davis in London.
subfiles.summary: Asks Davis to pass the article to Atherton for Embassy files.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Mukden oil-control despatch
subfiles.about: The note summarizes Texas Company’s request to store Korean reserves at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Reports possible withdrawal from Korea if the request is refused; no action is required.

subfiles.title: Chase cover despatch to the Secretary of State, first copy
subfiles.about: Chase forwards despatch No. 962 on Japanese oil controls.
subfiles.summary: Encloses a copy of his despatch to the American Minister at Peiping.

subfiles.title: Chase despatch No. 962, first copy
subfiles.about: Chase reports Texas Company’s proposed use of Dairen tanks for Korean oil reserves.
subfiles.summary: The company lacks enough storage in Korea and may leave that market if authorities reject its request.

subfiles.title: Chase cover despatch, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy forwards despatch No. 962.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cover for Chase’s despatch to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Chase despatch No. 962, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy reports Texas Company’s storage request.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the proposal to use Dairen tanks for stocks required in Korea.

subfiles.title: Chase cover despatch, third copy
subfiles.about: A third copy forwards despatch No. 962.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cover for Chase’s despatch to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Chase despatch No. 962, third copy
subfiles.about: A third copy reports Texas Company’s storage request.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the possible use of Dairen tanks and withdrawal from Korea if refused.

subfiles.title: Chase cover despatch, fourth copy
subfiles.about: A fourth copy forwards despatch No. 962.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cover for Chase’s despatch to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Chase despatch No. 962, fourth copy
subfiles.about: A fourth copy reports Texas Company’s storage request.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the Dairen storage proposal and possible end of the company’s Korean business.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 250
subfiles.about: The Netherlands Minister calls for a united foreign-company and governmental front.
subfiles.summary: He sees little prospect of improvement without coordinated American, British, and Dutch action.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 249 conveying Goold’s message
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, conveying J. C. Goold’s message
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for P. W. Parker
subfiles.about: Foreign oil representatives seek coordinated governmental support if they reject Japan’s stock rules.
subfiles.summary: Goold proposes simultaneous defensive warnings by the three governments. He also urges withholding requested Manchurian sales information and crude-oil quotations to avoid accepting the proposed monopoly.

subfiles.title: Outgoing notice to Tokyo on message delivery
subfiles.about: Washington reports that the company message is being mailed to Standard-Vacuum.
subfiles.summary: Advises Tokyo of transmission to the company.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck letter forwarding telegram No. 249
subfiles.about: Hornbeck forwards the Embassy telegram carrying Goold’s message.
subfiles.summary: Encloses a copy of Tokyo telegram No. 249.

subfiles.title: Parker letter quoting Yokohama cable
subfiles.about: Parker reports Japan’s explanation of quotas and a renewed demand for complete storage plans.
subfiles.summary: The cable summarizes Japan’s position on refining, pricing, and sales. Parker says submitting the form by November 15 would effectively accept costly storage obligations and asks for information on Japan’s Manchurian-monopoly reply.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck–Parker telephone conversation
subfiles.about: Hornbeck and Parker discuss oil supply reports, company travel, and possible diplomatic coordination.
subfiles.summary: Parker distinguishes companies supplying crude oil to Japan and describes planned visits by foreign oil executives. They discuss Dutch–Japanese trade talks, possible suspension of Japan’s petroleum law, and the absence of a British governmental proposal.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck–Parker conversation before Parker’s departure
subfiles.about: Parker asks whether the United States might restrict petroleum exports.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says he expects no such action without a decision by higher authorities and reiterates that Washington awaits British initiative. He expects diplomats to assist company talks in Tokyo and privately advises Parker to consider Japan’s growing preference for domestic refining and distribution.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck–Teagle telephone conversation
subfiles.about: Teagle asks for developments and advice before Parker travels to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck advises caution about long-term oil-delivery commitments and attention to Dutch–Japanese trade negotiations.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 251 correcting telegram No. 241, first copy
subfiles.about: Grew corrects the capital threshold for favorable refinery permission.
subfiles.summary: The company must have not less than half Japanese capital.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 251, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy repeats the correction to telegram No. 241.
subfiles.summary: Repeats the “not less than half Japanese capital” wording.

subfiles.title: Document file note for despatch No. 1007
subfiles.about: The note points to another file location for Grew’s despatch No. 1007.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references file 894.00P.R/82 and an excerpt on American oil interests.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan, excerpt from despatch No. 1007
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes foreign companies’ uncertainty under Japan’s petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: It reports Japan’s aim to replace imports of finished petroleum products with domestic refining. American and British firms seek clarity before investing in six-month stocks, while their governments have made representations. The excerpt continues beyond page 154.
